method: A helix radiates along its axis when the circumference is about one wavelength and the turns are spaced by roughly a quarter wavelength; this is the axial mode, and it is circularly polarised, with the winding hand setting the polarisation. The page takes the winding the user enters rather than proposing one. The wavelength is the speed of light over the frequency, expressed in the chosen length unit; the electrical circumference is the winding circumference, pi times the diameter, over that wavelength, and the electrical spacing is the centre-to-centre turn spacing over it in the same way. The classical Kraus estimate of the gain is fifteen times the square of the electrical circumference times the turns times the electrical spacing, in linear terms, reported in dBi, which reduces to 3.45 times the number of turns when the circumference is one wavelength and the spacing is 0.23 of it. The half-power beamwidth is fifty-two degrees over the electrical circumference times the square root of the turns times the electrical spacing. The pitch angle is the arctangent of the spacing over the circumference, and the winding length is the turns times the spacing. Those estimates assume a circular ground plane with a rim and an optimum pitch and read several decibels high against a flat ground plane, so the page prints them as a design target. A circumference outside 0.75 to 1.33 wavelengths, a pitch outside 12 to 15 degrees and fewer than three turns each raise a warning and still return a figure. Units are labels for the lengths the user enters. It refuses a blank, non-numeric or non-positive frequency, diameter or spacing, a frequency outside 0.1 to 300000 MHz, fewer than one or more than one thousand turns, and any unit other than millimetres or inches, naming the field in each message. Nothing is sent, stored or uploaded.
